security_topic: post-authentication redirect to original URL after SSO login
question_text:
When a user accesses a direct Jenkins resource (e.g., a job URL) and their session has expired, Jenkins correctly redirects them to authenticate via SSO. However, after successful authentication, Jenkins redirects the user to the dashboard/home page (/) instead of the originally requested URL.

answer_text:

Author: VenuReddy3129
Date: 2026-05-28T09:33:30Z
Labels: 
State: closed

[c0]
### Jenkins and plugins versions report

Jenkins incorrectly redirects users to the dashboard (/) instead of the requested job URL:

On first access to any Jenkins URL
After session timeout (~30 minutes) and re-authentication

The correct page only loads on the second attempt.

When a user accesses a direct Jenkins resource (e.g., a job URL) and their session has expired, Jenkins correctly redirects them to authenticate via SSO. However, after successful authentication, Jenkins redirects the user to the dashboard/home page (/) instead of the originally requested URL.
This results in a poor user experience because users must manually re-navigate to the intended job.

### What Operating System are you using (both controller, and any agents involved in the problem)?

Jenkins: 2.541.3
Auth: miniOrange SAML plugin (v3.4.2)
Browser: Edge
Behind reverse proxy

### Reproduction steps

Open a direct Jenkins job URL:
https://jenkins.example.com/job/sample-job/



Ensure the user session is expired:

Either wait for idle timeout (~30 minutes)
Or manually clear session cookies



The user is redirected to the SSO login page.


Complete authentication successfully.


Observe redirect behavior:

User is redirected to:
https://jenkins.example.com/

instead of:
https://jenkins.example.com/job/sample-job/





If the user again navigates to the same job URL manually, it loads correctly.

### Expected Results

After successful authentication, Jenkins should redirect the user back to the originally requested URL (e.g., /job/sample-job/), preserving user context.

### Actual Results

After authentication, Jenkins always redirects to the dashboard (/), ignoring the original request URL.

title: Add native BeanShell scripting support to Jenkins core
need_summary: Whether native BeanShell scripting in Jenkins core would need sandboxing and be restricted so only administrators can use it, as noted in the script security discussion and the linked plugin repository.
security_topic: security restrictions for adding BeanShell scripting support in Jenkins
question_text:
### What feature do you want to see added?

Currently, Jenkins only provides native Groovy support through its Script Console and Pipeline DSL. BeanShell is a mature, actively maintained Java scripting language that offers POSIX-compatible scripting capabilities, making it a portable alternative to platform-specific scripts such as `.cmd`, `.sh` or `.ps1`.

This is not intended as a replacement for Groovy, but as a complement to it, allowing both languages to work together within the same pipeline, giving users the flexibility to leverage the strengths of each one.

Having native BeanShell support in Jenkins core would allow users to write portable build and deployment scripts that run consistently across different operating systems without requiring platform-specific interpreters, while also providing the ability to use BeanShell files (`.bsh`), allowing separation of concerns between the pipeline and the POSIX commands used, as is done with Command Scripts (`.cmd`), Bash Scripts (`.sh`) or PowerShell Scripts (`.ps1`).
answer_text: Use of that library should be restricted to controllers where every user, including every committer to every repo with a `Jenkinsfile`, is an administrator. It also doesn't support distributed builds at all.

question_text:
The Bitbucket OAuth Plugin sends the OAuth2 access token as an access_token query string parameter instead of using the Authorization: Bearer header. ### What Operating System are you using (both controller, and any agents involved in the problem)?

The Bitbucket OAuth Plugin sends the OAuth2 access token as an access_token query string parameter instead of using the Authorization: Bearer header. This is because the plugin uses Scribe 1.3.3, whose OAuth20ServiceImpl.signRequest() method defaults to request.addQuerystringParameter(OAuthConstants.ACCESS_TOKEN, accessToken.getToken()), and the plugin's BitbucketOAuth20Service inner class in BitbucketApiV2.java does not override signRequest().
Bitbucket Cloud has announced CHANGE-3052, which deprecates passing OAuth access tokens via query parameters or POST body. Brownouts began April 20, 2026, and full enforcement is May 4, 2026, after which this plugin will be permanently broken.

Affected Code
File: src/main/java/org/jenkinsci/plugins/api/BitbucketApiV2.java
The inner class BitbucketOAuth20Service (line 43) extends OAuth20ServiceImpl but does not override signRequest(). The inherited implementation sends the token as a query parameter:

// Inherited from org.scribe.oauth.OAuth20ServiceImpl (Scribe 1.3.3)
public void signRequest(Token accessToken, OAuthRequest request) {
    request.addQuerystringParameter(OAuthConstants.ACCESS_TOKEN, accessToken.getToken());
}
This causes all API calls in BitbucketApiService.java (lines 68 and 85) to send requests like:

GET https://api.bitbucket.org/2.0/user?access_token=XXXXX
GET https://api.bitbucket.org/2.0/user/workspaces?access_token=XXXXX
Instead of:

GET https://api.bitbucket.org/2.0/user
Authorization: Bearer XXXXX

### Reproduction steps

 1.  Install Jenkins v2.516.3 (or any recent version)
 2.  Install Bitbucket OAuth Plugin v0.16
 3.  Configure Bitbucket OAuth Plugin with a valid Bitbucket OAuth consumer (Client ID and Client Secret)
 4.  Configure Jenkins to use "Bitbucket OAuth Plugin" as the Security Realm
 5.  Log out of Jenkins
 6.  Attempt to log in via Bitbucket OAuth during a CHANGE-3052 brownout window (see schedule below) or after May 4, 2026

[c1] @MilanTyagi2004 2026-04-01T07:08:57Z:
Hi @salomj,

I’d like to take this issue.

From what I understand, this behavior is a side-effect of the fix introduced in SECURITY-3657, where Jenkins now blocks extraction of archives if a symlink exists anywhere in the path to prevent arbitrary file write vulnerabilities .

### Problem Breakdown

* `stash` allows symlinks to be archived.
* `unstash` fails because extraction now rejects any path containing symlinks.
* This breaks valid workflows (e.g., Lerna / node_modules) where symlinks are expected and safe.

### Proposed Approach

I’m considering the following directions:

1. **Handle symlinks during stash (preferred)**

   * Detect symlinks while creating the stash archive
   * Either:

     * Skip them with a warning, or
     * Store metadata instead of raw symlinks

2. **Safe extraction validation**

   * Allow symlinks only if:

     * They resolve within the workspace
     * They don’t escape the target directory
   * This preserves security guarantees while allowing valid use cases

3. **Optional configuration (fallback)**

   * Introduce a flag like `allowSafeSymlinks`
   * Default remains secure, but users can opt-in for controlled environments

### Goal

Maintain the security guarantees introduced by SECURITY-3657 while restoring compatibility for common development workflows that rely on symlinks.

Let me know if this direction sounds good, or if you’d prefer a stricter approach (e.g., always skipping symlinks during stash).

Hi @salomj,

I’d like to take this issue.

From what I understand, this behavior is a side-effect of the fix introduced in SECURITY-3657, where Jenkins now blocks extraction of archives if a symlink exists anywhere in the path to prevent arbitrary file write vulnerabilities .

### Problem Breakdown

* `stash` allows symlinks to be archived.
* `unstash` fails because extraction now rejects any path containing symlinks.
* This breaks valid workflows (e.g., Lerna / node_modules) where symlinks are expected and safe.

### Proposed Approach

I’m considering the following directions:

1. **Handle symlinks during stash (preferred)**

   * Detect symlinks while creating the stash archive
   * Either:

     * Skip them with a warning, or
     * Store metadata instead of raw symlinks

2. **Safe extraction validation**

   * Allow symlinks only if:

     * They resolve within the workspace
     * They don’t escape the target directory
   * This preserves security guarantees while allowing valid use cases

3. **Optional configuration (fallback)**

   * Introduce a flag like `allowSafeSymlinks`
   * Default remains secure, but users can opt-in for controlled environments

### Goal

Maintain the security guarantees introduced by SECURITY-3657 while restoring compatibility for common development workflows that rely on symlinks.

Let me know if this direction sounds good, or if you’d prefer a stricter approach (e.g., always skipping symlinks during stash).

I can start with a PR once aligned.

title: Fenced-in Admin
need_summary: Whether fencing Admin rights into limited categories is supported, with the answer anchored in Jenkins JEP 223 stating that features that cannot elevate permissions should use Overall/Manage permission.
security_topic: permission scoping and privilege escalation via admin-like features
question_text: I would like to see the ability to grant Admin rights to a user, but fence them into specific categories of configuration. For example, on a shared Jenkins site you don't want to grant Admin rights to users and risk exposing projects others should not see. But that also prevents users from creating Cloud Nodes that use Docker images as slaves.
answer_text:
This is what Overall/Manage permission is for: https://www.jenkins.io/jep/223

Anything that cannot be used to elevate one's own permission to Administer should ultimately use Manage. The problem is that many features can be used in that way. If a feature you want them "fenced in" like that can be used to elevate permissions, it's not suitable.

Quick investigation in core/src/main/java/jenkins/model/run/KeepRunAction.java  the action factory does emit Keep/UnKeep entries when new-build-page.flag is enabled, gated on target.canToggleLogKeep() and target.hasPermission(Permission.UPDATE) / Permission.DELETE. title: Race condition in HudsonPrivateSecurityRealm.doCreateFirstAccount allows multiple initial admin accounts
need_summary: Whether the reported race condition in HudsonPrivateSecurityRealm.doCreateFirstAccount can create multiple initial admin accounts, and the answer rests on the linked PR https://github.com/jenkinsci/jenkins/pull/26036 and the synchronized lock code it proposes.
security_topic: race condition in initial admin account creation
question_text: A race condition exists in `HudsonPrivateSecurityRealm.doCreateFirstAccount`. The `hasSomeUser()` check is non-atomic and unsynchronized. In testing with 20 concurrent threads, 20 different user accounts were created, and all 20 were granted administrative privileges via `tryToMakeAdmin(u)`.
answer_text:
I opened a PR that makes the first account creation atomic by synchronizing the check and creation logic on a dedicated lock, ensuring that only one initial admin user can be created:

https://github.com/jenkinsci/jenkins/pull/26036

### What Operating System are you using (both controller, and any agents involved in the problem)? Fedora 43 ### Reproduction steps 1. Initialize a clean Jenkins installation using `HudsonPrivateSecurityRealm` as the security realm. 2. Ensure no user accounts have been created yet (initial setup state). 3. Simultaneously send multiple concurrent POST requests to the `/securityRealm/createFirstAccount` endpoint with different usernames and valid account details. 4. Verify the number of users created and their permissions. ### Expected Results Only the very first request should succeed in creating an account. All subsequent concurrent requests should fail with a 401 Unauthorized error (or similar) because a user already exists or is being created, preventing the creation of multiple initial administrator accounts. ### Actual Results A race condition exists in `HudsonPrivateSecurityRealm.doCreateFirstAccount`. The `hasSomeUser()` check is non-atomic and unsynchronized. In testing with 20 concurrent threads, 20 different user accounts were created, and all 20 were granted administrative privileges via `tryToMakeAdmin(u)`. ### Anything else? The vulnerability is a classic Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use race condition in `core/src/main/java/hudson/security/HudsonPrivateSecurityRealm.java` between lines 366-376. While impact is limited to the initial setup phase, it allows an attacker to gain admin access if they can time requests during the window before the first user is fully persisted. ### Are you interested in contributing a fix? Yes, the fix involves adding a static lock object to synchronize the `doCreateFirstAccount` method. This ensures the `hasSomeUser()` check and subsequent user creation are atomic. --- COMMENTS --- [c1] @Pnkcaht 2026-01-03T02:26:16Z: Hi, I was able to reproduce the issue during the initial setup by sending multiple concurrent POST requests to `/securityRealm/createFirstAccount`. The method `doCreateFirstAccount` checks `hasSomeUser()` and then creates the user without any synchronization, which allows a race condition where multiple requests can pass the check before the first user is persisted. I opened a PR that makes the first account creation atomic by synchronizing the check and creation logic on a dedicated lock, ensuring that only one initial admin user can be created: https://github.com/jenkinsci/jenkins/pull/26036 ```java /** * Lock used to make initial admin account creation atomic. */ private static final Object CREATE_FIRST_ACCOUNT_LOCK = new Object(); /** * Creates a first admin user account. * *

* This can be run by anyone, but only to create the very first user account. */ @RequirePOST public void doCreateFirstAccount(StaplerRequest2 req, StaplerResponse2 rsp) throws IOException, ServletException { synchronized (CREATE_FIRST_ACCOUNT_LOCK) { if (hasSomeUser()) { rsp.sendError(SC_UNAUTHORIZED, "First user was already created"); return; } User u = createAccount(req, rsp, false, "firstUser.jelly"); if (u != null) { tryToMakeAdmin(u); loginAndTakeBack(req, rsp, u); } } } ``` --- [c2] @daniel-beck 2026-01-03T12:37:14Z: > The vulnerability I do not consider this to be a vulnerability, since the user was clearly entitled to perform the action. They could just run a Groovy script instead. The outcome (multiple admin users) might be surprising, but it's unlikely to occur. Realistically, the current approach going from no users to having the Jenkins security realm set up is a little awkward. Note that, if this were a vulnerability, this wouldn't be the place to report it. ---

### What Operating System are you using (both controller, and any agents involved in the problem)?

Fedora 43

### Reproduction steps

   1. Initialize a clean Jenkins installation using `HudsonPrivateSecurityRealm` as the security realm.
   2. Ensure no user accounts have been created yet (initial setup state).
   3. Simultaneously send multiple concurrent POST requests to the `/securityRealm/createFirstAccount` endpoint with different usernames and valid account details.
   4. Verify the number of users created and their permissions.


### Expected Results

Only the very first request should succeed in creating an account. All subsequent concurrent requests should fail with a 401 Unauthorized error (or similar) because a user already exists or is being created, preventing the creation of multiple initial administrator accounts.

### Actual Results

A race condition exists in `HudsonPrivateSecurityRealm.doCreateFirstAccount`. The `hasSomeUser()` check is non-atomic and unsynchronized. In testing with 20 concurrent threads, 20 different user accounts were created, and all 20 were granted administrative privileges via `tryToMakeAdmin(u)`.

### Anything else?

The vulnerability is a classic Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use race condition in `core/src/main/java/hudson/security/HudsonPrivateSecurityRealm.java` between lines 366-376. While impact is limited to the initial setup phase, it allows an attacker to gain admin access if they can time requests during the window before the first user is fully persisted.

### Are you interested in contributing a fix?

Yes, the fix involves adding a static lock object to synchronize the `doCreateFirstAccount` method. This ensures the `hasSomeUser()` check and subsequent user creation are atomic.

`java -jar jenkins.war --requestFormContentSize=-1`

comments.author: mawinter69
comments.body:
hmm, actually by default the form contentsize is not limited in winstone.
See https://github.com/jenkinsci/winstone/blob/b51575433e8ad9e01d47fb23b339fe760d14c0d7/src/main/java/winstone/cmdline/Option.java#L100 and https://github.com/jenkinsci/winstone/blob/b51575433e8ad9e01d47fb23b339fe760d14c0d7/src/main/java/winstone/HostConfiguration.java#L179

So you should check whether you set the option `requestFormContentSize` when starting Jenkins. If yes either remove that or increase it.

comments.author: MarkEWaite
comments.body:
Thanks for the report.  I can duplicate the issue if I create a freestyle project with your list of plugins and paste the complete text of ["A Christmas Carol"](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/46/pg46.txt) into the Execute shell step.  Jenkins 2.531 accepts that large amount of text, while Jenkins 2.538 and 2.542 do not.

Jenkins 2.531 bundles winstone 8.13.1 with Eclipse Jetty 12.0.25.  Jenkins 2.538 bundles winstone 8.1023.v8b_42b_1b_79b_f7 with Eclipse Jetty 12.1.4.

I'm able to avoid the issue by running Jenkins with the command:

```
java -Dorg.eclipse.jetty.server.Request.maxFormContentSize=3000000 -jar jenkins.war
```

In case you're interested, there are issues with several of the plugins installed on your controller.  Those plugins don't affect this issue, but they may affect the long term health of your Jenkins controller.

I had to disable the Atlassian Bitbucket integration plugin in order to see the failure.

There are many plugins in your plugin list that are deprecated or no longer useful.  They should be removed.  The message says:

comments.author: MarkEWaite
comments.body:
@olamy this seems to be a change in behavior between Jetty 12.0 and Jetty 12.1.  I think that we'll want to make a change in winstone to adapt to this change in Jetty.  I think that we'll need to backport it to the Jenkins 2.541.1 LTS in time for the LTS release candidate Jan 7, 2026.

If you're available to help with understanding what changed between Jetty 12.0 and Jetty 12.1 with regard to `org.eclipse.jetty.server.Request.maxFormContentSize`, that would be great.  The [Jetty 12.1.x documentation page](https://github.com/jetty/jetty.project/blob/jetty-12.1.x/documentation/jetty/modules/programming-guide/pages/security/configuring-form-size.adoc) on form size was updated in January of this year for the Jetty 12.1 releases.

comments.author: MarkEWaite
comments.body:
> You should be able to workaround your problem by setting `requestFormContentSize` to a large value

You're right!  Thanks!  The online help for `java -jar jenkins.war --help` does not mention `--requestFormContentSize` as an accepted argument, but it works.  I confirmed it works with the command line:

`java -jar jenkins.war --requestFormContentSize=3000000`

I confirmed it fails with the command line:

`java -jar jenkins.war --requestFormContentSize=-1`

comments.author: daniel-beck
comments.body:
@timja Thanks.

This seems to be due to https://github.com/KostyaSha/github-integration-plugin/blob/358149f481dc8735c89d099da451af8903049f3d/github-pullrequest-plugin/src/main/resources/org/jenkinsci/plugins/github/pullrequest/GitHubPRRepository/index.groovy#L41 if Content Security Policy is being enforced. Disable CSP enforcement again for now, you're using a plugin not yet compatible (and already known to not be compatible).

Docs, just in case: https://www.jenkins.io/doc/book/security/csp/

As the plugin tracks issues outside the `jenkinsci` org, I'm closing this one.
